comment: Privacy jurisdictions, and the one behaviour that depends on them.
Consumers must not switch on the raw jurisdiction value. They ask a single
derived question -- does this jurisdiction require prior opt-in before a
device may transmit? -- and the answer lives here, in one file that both C++
(src/non-gpl/CapeUtils) and PHP (the setup wizard, the statistics client)
read. The same pattern as settings.json and interface-settings.json, and for
the same reason: a policy re-listed in each consumer drifts.
'priorOptIn' is true only where a regime actually demands consent before
transmission. That is the EU/EEA (GDPR + ePrivacy) and the UK (UK GDPR +
PECR, functionally identical since 2020). It is deliberately NOT the rest of
the world: CCPA/CPRA is an opt-out regime for sale and sharing rather than
opt-in for telemetry, PIPEDA accepts implied consent for non-sensitive data,
and the Australian APPs very probably do not bind a project this size.
Applying EU mechanics to users those rules do not cover protects nobody and
makes FPP worse for them.
'priorOptInDefault' is what an unrecognised value means. It is false: the
strict path is taken on a positive match, not by accident.
'countryCodes' is used only by the 'Lookup' buttons on the setup wizard's
locale step, which the user presses deliberately. A geoip lookup already
returns the country, so throwing it away and inferring from the time zone
instead would be strictly worse. It is a SEED, exactly like the timezone
inference: it fills the field in, the user sees it, and the user can change
it before anything is saved.
The EU list is the 27 member states plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway.
Those three are EEA rather than EU, the GDPR reaches them, and geoip
providers' 'in_eu' flags do NOT cover them -- which is exactly why the list
is written down here rather than delegated to whatever the lookup says.
The UK entry carries the Crown Dependencies for the same kind of reason.
Note geoip resolves the PUBLIC IP, so it reports where the device reaches
the internet, not where the device is. For a value the user is shown and
can correct that is fine; it is not good enough to act on unattended, and
nothing does.
'timezonePrefix' is used only when LegalJurisdiction has never been answered.
Every device already has a TimeZone, so an unanswered box in Europe still
gets the strict path while the rest of the fleet does not have to wait for a
prompt. The inference is never written to the settings file, and an actual
answer always wins over it.
Prefix matching is LONGEST MATCH FIRST: 'Europe/London' must resolve to UK,
not to EU via the shorter 'Europe/' entry. Both are strict, so nothing
behaves differently today, but the inferred value should still be right.
The Europe/ catch-all is deliberately over-inclusive: it pulls in Switzerland
and other non-EEA European zones, which then take the strict path they do not
strictly need. That is the safe direction for a guess, and it only ever
applies until the user answers.
NOT represented here on purpose: US-CA. California's CCPA/CPRA would not
change what the privacy step does. California's SB-327 *is* relevant, but to
device credentials rather than to privacy, and the security step is uniform
everywhere precisely because that law and UK PSTI point the other way.
